references.authors: Schymanski, E.L.; Jeon, J.; Gulde, R.; Fenner, K.; Ruff, M.; Singer, H.P.; Hollender, J.
references.title: Identifying Small Molecules via High Resolution Mass Spectrometry: Communicating Confidence
references.verification: Crossref works record and PubMed PMID 24476540 retrieved in this session; title matches. Neither source has an abstract (2-page viewpoint), so the content fields summarise the standard five-level scheme rather than text read in this session.
references.problem: How to communicate the confidence of HRMS small-molecule identifications consistently across labs.
references.data: Viewpoint with illustrative environmental HRMS cases; no benchmark dataset.
references.method: Five-level scale: L1 confirmed structure (reference standard), L2 probable structure (library or diagnostic evidence), L3 tentative candidate(s), L4 unequivocal formula, L5 exact mass of interest.
references.uncertainty_method: Qualitative evidence levels only; no quantitative treatment of RT deviations or tolerances.
references.transfer_setting: Not addressed; Level 1 presupposes an authentic standard measured on the lab's own chromatographic system.
references.main_results: Became the de facto NTS reporting standard. Predicted-RT agreement does not reach Level 1; Kretschmer et al. 2026 call such matches 'almost level 1'.
references.limitations: Qualitative and not automatable; prescribes no RT tolerance and does not quantify ambiguity within the candidate space (critique by Metz et al. 2025).
references.relevance_to_study: Positions our calibrated RT windows as auditable Level-3 candidate elimination and ranking evidence, filling the RT criterion the scheme leaves unspecified.

references.authors: Aalizadeh, R.; Nika, M.-C.; Thomaidis, N.S.
references.title: Development and application of retention time prediction models in the suspect and non-target screening of emerging contaminants
references.verification: Crossref record and PubMed PMID 30312924 (abstract) retrieved; title matches. Full text not accessible (Elsevier), so the window values are unknown.
references.category: QSRR RT prediction with error windows for suspect/NTS
references.problem: Predict tR of emerging contaminants to support suspect and non-target identification in HILIC- and RPLC-HRMS.
references.data: 682 compounds by HILIC-ESI(+); RPLC sets of 1830 (ESI+) and 308 (ESI-) compounds.
references.method: Support-vector-machine QSRR models with applicability-domain assessment.
references.uncertainty_method: Monte Carlo sampling used both for the applicability domain and to derive 'acceptable error windows' for predicted tR (numeric windows not in the abstract).
references.transfer_setting: System-specific models; the abstract states the error windows were computed for predicted tR 'from various LC conditions'.
references.main_results: Validated HILIC/RPLC tR models were applied to identify transformation products of emerging contaminants and biocides in wastewater and sludge.
references.limitations: Error windows are fixed per model rather than candidate-adaptive or finite-sample valid, and the models are tied to the training LC conditions.
references.relevance_to_study: Typical of the heuristic 'acceptable error window' practice that our jackknife+ conformal windows replace.

references.authors: Aalizadeh, R.; Alygizakis, N.A.; Schymanski, E.L.; Krauss, M.; Schulze, T.; Ibáñez, M.; McEachran, A.D.; Chao, A.; Williams, A.J.; Gago-Ferrero, P.; Covaci, A.; Moschet, C.; Young, T.M.; Hollender, J.; Slobodnik, J.; Thomaidis, N.S.
references.title: Development and Application of Liquid Chromatographic Retention Time Indices in HRMS-Based Suspect and Nontarget Screening
references.verification: Crossref record and PubMed PMID 34382770 (abstract) retrieved; title matches. Implementation details come from the Malm & Kruve 2025 and Hupatz 2025 PMC full texts.
references.problem: Make LC retention data comparable between laboratories as supporting evidence in suspect/NTS identification.
references.data: 2123 compounds used to select two sets of 18 calibrants (ESI+ and ESI-); external validation on other instruments and LC conditions, coordinated by NORMAN.
references.method: Calibrant-based RTI scale (1-1000) plus two QSRR models that predict RTI with applicability domains, used to remove false-positive annotations; online calculator rti.chem.uoa.gr.
references.uncertainty_method: QSRR applicability domain. Downstream users apply residual cut-offs, e.g. ±2 standardized residuals (Hupatz et al. 2025).
references.transfer_setting: Users measure the calibrant mix on their own system; RT is rescaled linearly between the first- and last-eluting calibrant (per Malm & Kruve 2025).
references.main_results: The RTI system was validated externally and improved confidence and inter-lab comparability in two suspect/NTS examples. It can also check LC reproducibility.
references.code_available: Web platform http://rti.chem.uoa.gr/ (source code not stated).
references.limitations: Linear first/last-calibrant scaling ignores gradient nonlinearity: a GAM on all calibrants cut inter-system suspect RMSE from 150.4 to 78.1 RTI units (Malm & Kruve 2025). The windows are not coverage-calibrated.
references.relevance_to_study: The community-standard calibrant protocol. Our monotone isotonic+PCHIP calibrant mapping generalises RTI scaling, and our conformal windows supply the calibrated tolerance it lacks.

references.title: Do experimental projection methods outcompete retention time prediction models in non-target screening? A case study on LC/HRMS interlaboratory comparison data
references.verification: Crossref record, PubMed PMID 40671565 and the PMC12268317 full text were read. The ESI zip was downloaded via the Europe PMC supplementaryFiles endpoint and its file list and CSV header were inspected.
references.category: multi-system benchmark of RT projection vs ML prediction for NTS
references.problem: Do calibrant-based projection methods or ML RT prediction better estimate candidate RTs across chromatographic systems used in NTS?
references.data: NORMAN interlaboratory data: 41 calibrants and 45 suspects on 38 systems, 37 of them reversed-phase (1332 ordered system pairs). The paper reports 12-39 detected calibrants and 17-40 detected suspects per system.
references.method: RT-to-RTI scaling; pairwise GAM projection on calibrants detected in both systems; xgbTree (Mordred descriptors) trained on 1795 external Athens RTs, then projected via calibrants. Methods compared by RMSE and F-tests.
references.uncertainty_method: RMSE, MAD and the 95th percentile of absolute deviations. Recommends ±2 RMSE estimated on independent QC chemicals as an approximately 95% window.
references.transfer_setting: Source-to-target projection using the calibrants common to both systems; suspects held out from fitting.
references.main_results: Projection RMSE was 78.1 RTI units vs 149.0 for prediction. Projection was significantly better in 71.5% of system pairs and prediction in 2.4%. Mobile-phase pH/additive and column chemistry dominated the disagreements. Calibrant RMSE was a poor proxy for suspect RMSE (R² = 0.30).
references.code_available: Yes. Data, R Markdown code and results are in the ESI (RSC; Europe PMC supplementary files).
references.limitations: Only 37 acidic reversed-phase systems and 82 chemicals; no candidate-level filtering or coverage evaluation; GAM projection unavailable for 9.8% of suspects eluting outside the calibrant range.
references.relevance_to_study: Shows calibrant residuals underestimate suspect errors, which motivates our meta-learned difficulty normalisation. It also provides a downloadable external test set (37 systems, common calibrants) for coverage and width checks.

references.title: Candidate Structure Prioritization in Non-Target Screening with Predicted Collision Cross-Sections and Uncertainty Quantification
references.venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
references.verification: Crossref record (and ChemRxiv preprint 10.26434/chemrxiv.15006479/v1), PubMed PMID 42789453 and the PMC13663483 full text were read.
references.problem: Replace heuristic relative-CCS thresholds with candidate prioritisation that has a statistical guarantee on retaining true structures.
references.data: METLIN-CCS (27,377 SMILES; 58,041 ion species) for training and calibration. External in-silico NTS sets from EnvCCS and AllCCS used SIRIUS+CSI:FingerID top-10 candidates (12,464 and 5274 candidates).
references.method: Normalized Mondrian (by ion type) conformal predictive system wrapped around GraphCCS. The error function is the mean MCES distance to the k nearest training compounds; candidates are kept if P_CCS ≥ α. Includes conformal OOD detection.
references.uncertainty_method: Conformal predictive distributions normalised by a similarity-based difficulty function, giving recall ≥ 100-α in-domain, plus calibration-conditional correction (δ = 0.05).
references.transfer_setting: No instrument or system shift. Calibration uses about 1500 library ions per taxonomy from METLIN-CCS; only in-domain candidates (P_OOD ≤ 90%) are evaluated.
references.main_results: Recall guarantees held in-domain on the external sets. At 90% recall only about 16% of incorrect candidates were removed (at most 8% above random), and only 49% (EnvCCS) and 31% (AllCCS) of ions were in-domain.
references.limitations: CCS discriminates isomers poorly; the OOD threshold is heuristic without theory; a large same-distribution calibration set is required; no RT and no cross-laboratory shift.
references.relevance_to_study: The closest methodological precedent: the same normalised-conformal 'retain ≥ 1-α true structures' logic for NTS, which the authors propose extending to RT. We provide that RT extension under few-calibrant system transfer.

references.authors: Metz, T.O.; Chang, C.H.; Gautam, V.; Anjum, A.; Tian, S.; Wang, F.; Colby, S.M.; Nunez, J.R.; Blumer, M.R.; Edison, A.S.; Fiehn, O.; Jones, D.P.; Li, S.; Morgan, E.T.; Patti, G.J.; Ross, D.H.; Shapiro, M.R.; Williams, A.J.; Wishart, D.S.
references.title: Introducing 'Identification Probability' for Automated and Transferable Assessment of Metabolite Identification Confidence in Metabolomics and Related Studies
references.verification: Crossref record (with abstract), PubMed PMID 39699939 and the PMC11740175 full text were read.
references.problem: Quantify the ambiguity of metabolite identifications in an automated, platform-transferable way.
references.data: In-silico HMDB subsets (22,077 non-lipids; 44,537 lipids) with predicted m/z, CCS (CCSbase), RT (Retip; HILIC or RP) and MS/MS (CFM-ID 4.0).
references.method: Identification probability IP = 1/N, where N is the number of library compounds matching within user-set tolerances across all measured dimensions.
references.uncertainty_method: User-defined hard tolerances: RT ±0.1 or ±0.5 min; m/z ±0.1-5 ppm; CCS ±0.1-3%; MS/MS cosine ≥ 750-950.
references.transfer_setting: Assumes library properties are valid on the user's platform; no explicit RT transfer.
references.main_results: RT alone never gave unique matches at either tolerance. Adding RT to m/z, CCS and MS/MS raised the fraction of unambiguous matches, more so at ±0.1 min.
references.limitations: Hard tolerances ignore prediction uncertainty and heteroscedasticity; IP depends on library completeness; demonstration is purely in silico.
references.relevance_to_study: The RT tolerance directly sets the candidate count N, so our calibrated, candidate-specific windows give a principled tolerance for IP-style counting.

references.authors: Ngan, H.-L.; Turkina, V.; van Herwerden, D.; Yan, H.; Cai, Z.; Samanipour, S.
references.title: Machine Learning for Enhanced Identification Probability in RPLC/HRMS Nontargeted Workflows
references.verification: Crossref record, PubMed PMID 40791078 and the PMC12392258 full text were read.
references.category: learned true-positive probability using predicted RTI
references.problem: Raise identification probability of spectral-library matches in RPLC/HRMS NTA when retention information is missing.
references.data: 4713 calibrants on three harmonised RTI scales (fingerprint-to-RTI model); 485,577 MS/MS spectra (CNL-to-RTI model); 1,686,319 TP and semisynthetic TN matches; pesticide spikes in blanks and black-tea matrices.
references.method: Random-forest fingerprint-to-RTI and CNL-to-RTI regressors. A KNN classifier on the RTI discrepancy plus mass and spectral-match features gives P(TP); IP comes from averaged P(TP).
references.uncertainty_method: No intervals. The RTI discrepancy is a learned feature, with a leverage-based applicability domain and a P(TP) cut-off of 0.5.
references.transfer_setting: Calibrant-free: RTIs are inferred from the candidate structure and from the query spectrum, so no measured RT or system calibration is used.
references.main_results: Weighted F1 0.65 and MCC 0.30 in blanks. At P(TP) ≥ 0.5 the TP rate was 98.8% at an FP rate of 23.4%. IPs rose 46.7-54.5% over library matching alone.
references.limitations: Ignores the measured RT, so it cannot separate spectrally similar isomers by elution; large RTI errors (MAE 111 RTI units, MRE 27.5% on untrained calibrants) limit specificity.
references.relevance_to_study: An alternative soft-scoring route that is probabilistic but uncalibrated. Contrasts with our measured-RT conformal filter and could consume our window-based evidence.

references.authors: Bach, E.; Rogers, S.; Williamson, J.; Rousu, J.
references.title: Probabilistic framework for integration of mass spectrum and retention time information in small molecule identification
references.verification: Crossref record (with abstract), PubMed PMID 33244585 and the PMC8289373 full text were read.
references.problem: Combine MS-based candidate scores with retention information from all features of an LC-MS run to rank structures.
references.data: CASMI 2016 (208 MS2-RT tuples) and EA/MassBank (473 tuples). RankSVM trained on seven public RT datasets (four columns; H2O to MeOH with 0.1% formic acid).
references.method: Pairwise Markov random field: MS2 (IOKR) or MS1 node potentials, RankSVM retention-order edge potentials, max-marginals from random spanning-tree ensembles.
references.uncertainty_method: Platt-calibrated sigmoid on RankSVM margins; no RT intervals.
references.transfer_setting: Uses retention order, so absolute RT shifts are tolerated; the RankSVM was trained on RTs from other systems.
references.main_results: Significant top-k gains over MS2-only scoring and over the RT integrations of MetFrag 2.2 and the chain-graph method, including when only some features have MS2.
references.limitations: Order changes across different mobile phases or columns are not modelled; no candidate filtering or guarantee of retaining the true structure.
references.relevance_to_study: Precedent for cross-system retention-order learning in identification. Our pairwise-ranking base score builds on it but outputs calibrated per-candidate RT windows.

references.authors: Bach, E.; Schymanski, E.L.; Rousu, J.
references.title: Joint structural annotation of small molecules using liquid chromatography retention order and tandem mass spectrometry data
references.verification: Crossref record (with abstract) and bioRxiv API abstract (preprint 10.1101/2022.02.11.480137) retrieved; not indexed in PubMed; publisher full text not accessible.
references.category: structured prediction of annotations using retention order
references.problem: Jointly annotate all MS features of an LC-MS2 run using observed retention orders and MS2 scorer outputs.
references.data: All public reversed-phase LC-MS2 data in MassBank: 4,327 molecules from 18 LC conditions and 16 contributors.
references.method: LC-MS2Struct: a structured SVM combining CFM-ID, MetFrag and SIRIUS scores with observed retention orders, using stereochemistry-aware fingerprints.
references.transfer_setting: Uses retention orders within each LC condition; no absolute RT transfer.
references.main_results: Significantly higher annotation accuracy than earlier methods; improved the accuracy of state-of-the-art MS2 scorers by up to 106%.
references.code_available: Yes. Repositories aalto-ics-kepaco/msms_rt_ssvm and aalto-ics-kepaco/lcms2struct_exp were identified by web search but not opened.
references.limitations: Needs many co-measured features in a run; gives no per-candidate RT window or filtering guarantee; stereoisomers remain hard.
references.relevance_to_study: State of the art for soft retention-order integration, and a reference point for what calibrated absolute-RT windows add for single features and isomeric decoys.

references.authors: Ruttkies, C.; Schymanski, E.L.; Wolf, S.; Hollender, J.; Neumann, S.
references.title: MetFrag relaunched: incorporating strategies beyond in silico fragmentation
references.verification: Crossref record, PubMed PMID 26834843 and the PMC4732001 full text were read.
references.category: in-silico candidate ranking with an RT score
references.problem: Rank database candidates for HR-MS/MS spectra by combining in-silico fragmentation with metadata, including RT.
references.data: 473 merged HR-MS/MS spectra (Eawag/MassBank), plus three validation sets totalling 824 spectra.
references.method: Weighted sum of fragmenter, RT, reference and suspect scores. The RT score comes from a linear logP-RT fit on user standards (at least ten recommended) and a Gaussian density of the logP deviation with σ = 1.5.
references.uncertainty_method: Fixed Gaussian width σ = 1.5 logP units, described as 'chosen arbitrarily'; no calibration.
references.transfer_setting: In-situ calibration: standards measured on the user's own system fit the logP-RT model.
references.main_results: Top-1 ranks rose from 30 (MS/MS only, PubChem) to 336 (PubChem) and 420 (ChemSpider) when reference and RT information were added.
references.limitations: logP is a weak RT proxy for ionisable or polar compounds; the score width is arbitrary; the RT contribution is confounded with reference scores in the headline results.
references.relevance_to_study: The canonical NTS soft-scoring baseline with an ad hoc RT width. Our conformal scale can replace σ with a calibrated, candidate-adaptive width.

references.authors: Hupatz, H.; Rahu, I.; Wang, W.-C.; Peets, P.; Palm, E.H.; Kruve, A.
references.title: Critical review on in silico methods for structural annotation of chemicals detected with LC/HRMS non-targeted screening
references.verification: Crossref record (with abstract), PubMed PMID 39138659 and the PMC11700063 full text were read.
references.category: critical review and case study of NTS candidate prioritisation
references.problem: Review in-silico candidate retrieval and prioritisation (RT, CCS, ionisation) for LC/HRMS NTS and test them on real features.
references.data: Wastewater case study: 10 spiked chemicals and 10 unknown features; 515 unique candidates from MassBank, MetFrag, SIRIUS+CSI:FingerID and Spec2Mol.
references.method: Prioritisation with RTI-model RT using a ±2 standardized-residual cut-off and CCSbase CCS within 3%.
references.uncertainty_method: Fixed residual-based cut-offs; no coverage control.
references.transfer_setting: NORMAN RTI calibration to the lab's system.
references.main_results: The RT filter kept 255 of 515 candidates but deprioritised the correct structure for 2 of 10 spiked chemicals. Combining RT and CCS removed every candidate for 1 spiked and 2 unknown features.
references.code_available: Yes. github.com/kruvelab/NTS_LC_HRMS, plus an SI CSV of all candidates and prioritisation outcomes.
references.limitations: Only 20 features; RTI model applicability gaps (e.g. a boron-containing candidate could not be predicted); the authors attribute poor efficiency to high prediction uncertainty.
references.relevance_to_study: Documents both low efficiency and losses of true structures with heuristic RT cut-offs, and calls for uncertainty-aware evaluation metrics, which is our core motivation.

references.authors: McEachran, A.D.; Mansouri, K.; Newton, S.R.; Beverly, B.E.J.; Sobus, J.R.; Williams, A.J.
references.title: A comparison of three liquid chromatography (LC) retention time prediction models
references.verification: Crossref record, PubMed PMID 29501166 and the PMC6066181 full text were read.
references.category: RT-window filtering with measured true-positive loss
references.problem: Compare RT prediction models and RT screening windows for reducing candidate lists in non-targeted analysis.
references.data: 97 chemicals (78 training, 19 test) on an Eclipse Plus C8 45-min gradient; top-10 CompTox Dashboard candidates per test formula.
references.method: EPI Suite logP linear model vs ACD/ChromGenius vs OPERA-RT QSRR; candidates screened with ±2, ±3 and ±5 min windows.
references.uncertainty_method: Fixed absolute windows or fractions of run time (±5-20%); no calibration.
references.transfer_setting: Single in-house system; models trained on that system.
references.main_results: ±5 min removed about 20% of candidates while keeping 18/19 (ACD) and 17/19 (OPERA-RT) true chemicals. At ±3 min OPERA-RT removed 60% vs 40% but kept only 42% vs 83% of true chemicals. Zero-loss windows would have needed 5.06 and 6.5 min.
references.code_available: Not stated; training and test data and candidate tables in the supplementary material.
references.limitations: Very small training and test sets; one system; candidate lists pre-filtered to the top 10 by data-source count.
references.relevance_to_study: Quantifies the trade-off between removing false candidates and losing true positives with fixed windows, which motivates coverage-controlled windows and our recall-vs-elimination evaluation.

references.authors: Samaraweera, M.A.; Hall, L.M.; Hill, D.W.; Grant, D.F.
references.title: Evaluation of an Artificial Neural Network Retention Index Model for Chemical Structure Identification in Nontargeted Metabolomics
references.verification: Crossref DOI from the PubMed record (PMID 30350614) and the PMC8378237 full text were read; title matches.
references.category: RI filtering with similarity-adaptive windows and measured false-negative rate
references.problem: Remove false-positive candidates before in-silico MS/MS ranking using a predicted retention index.
references.data: 91 endogenous metabolites not in the RI training set; PubChem and HMDB candidate sets retrieved at ±15 ppm.
references.method: ANN retention-index model (C3-C14 n-amide scale); candidates outside the window removed before CFM-ID, CSI:FingerID, Mass Frontier or MetFrag ranking.
references.uncertainty_method: Windows of ±2SE (52.4 RIU) for candidates structurally similar to the training data (bit-key match) and ±3SE (78.6 RIU) otherwise, intended to give 95% sensitivity.
references.transfer_setting: Same-lab RI system anchored by n-amide homologues.
references.main_results: 12 of 91 true structures were eliminated (87% sensitivity, against 4-5 expected losses). The filter removed 58% of PubChem false candidates and roughly halved average ranks for three fragmenters. Widening by 0.5 SE gave 90% sensitivity at 53% specificity.
references.limitations: Single system, small test set, heuristic similarity bins; coverage particularly poor in the mid-RI range.
references.relevance_to_study: Direct evidence that nominal ±2SE windows under-cover and that novelty-aware widening helps. This is the gap our meta-learned difficulty normalisation with conformal calibration targets.

references.authors: Domingo-Almenara, X.; Guijas, C.; Billings, E.; Montenegro-Burke, J.R.; Uritboonthai, W.; Aisporna, A.E.; Chen, E.; Benton, H.P.; Siuzdak, G.
references.title: The METLIN small molecule dataset for machine learning-based retention time prediction
references.verification: Crossref record (with abstract), PubMed PMID 31862874 and the PMC6925099 full text were read.
references.category: RT prediction plus projection for candidate filtering and ranking
references.problem: Use a large RT dataset and deep learning for RT-based annotation across chromatographic methods.
references.data: METLIN SMRT (80,038 molecules); projections to four PredRet RP methods (plus others with at least 20 KEGG molecules); HMDB KEGG subset (6823) as candidates.
references.method: Deep-learning RT model on ECFP; predicted-to-experimental projection fitted on 50 randomly chosen known molecules; candidates filtered by a ROC-optimised relative RT-error threshold and ranked by RT error.
references.transfer_setting: Projection from the SMRT method to target methods using 50 known molecules.
references.main_results: The thresholds filtered out 31%, 41%, 36% and 21% of correct identities on the four systems. The correct identity was in the top 3 in about 70% of cases (41-45% with 18,457 HMDB candidates). Thresholds varied strongly between calibrant draws.
references.code_available: SMRT dataset openly released; model code availability not verified.
references.limitations: Needs about 50 identified molecules; filtering AUC only 0.65-0.69; the authors judge predicted-experimental RT filtering 'not a robust approach'.
references.relevance_to_study: Quantifies true-positive loss and calibrant-draw instability of naive RT thresholds after projection, the failure mode our leave-one-out-refitted jackknife+ windows control.

references.authors: García, C.A.; Gil-de-la-Fuente, A.; Barbas, C.; Otero, A.
references.title: Probabilistic metabolite annotation using retention time prediction and meta-learned projections
references.verification: PubMed PMID 35672784 (DOI and title match) and the PMC9172150 full text were read.
references.category: meta-learned few-calibrant projection with uncertainty for candidate ranking
references.problem: Exploit SMRT-trained RT predictions for annotation on other chromatographic methods using only a few identified molecules.
references.data: SMRT (80,038 RTs) for the RT models. PredRet methods for meta-learning, with targets FEM long, FEM orbitrap plasma, LIFE old and RIKEN held out in turn. HMDB KEGG (6823) as candidate database.
references.method: DNN RT predictor plus a Bayesian meta-learned Gaussian-process projection (prior learned on the other methods) fitted to 10-50 stratified calibrants; candidates ranked by z = |y - μ|/σ.
references.uncertainty_method: GP posterior predictive intervals assessed with the (scaled) interval score; z-score ranking.
references.main_results: The meta-learned GP projection was the most stable with few calibrants; the correct molecule was in the top three after z-scoring for 68% of mass queries with more than three candidates.
references.limitations: Gaussian, model-based intervals with no finite-sample coverage guarantee; σ depends on the projected RT, not on molecule-specific difficulty; only four target methods.
references.relevance_to_study: The closest prior work on meta-learning across chromatographic systems for few-calibrant RT transfer evaluated with the interval score. We add distribution-free jackknife+ coverage and molecule-level meta-learned difficulty.

references.authors: Kretschmer, F.; Harrieder, E.-M.; Witting, M.; Böcker, S.
references.title: Times are changing but order matters: transferable prediction of small-molecule liquid chromatography retention times
references.verification: Crossref record (with abstract; ChemRxiv preprint 10.26434/chemrxiv-2024-wd5j8), PubMed PMID 42823457 and the PMC13736644 full text were read.
references.category: transferable RT prediction via a condition-aware retention-order index
references.problem: Predict RTs for an arbitrary reversed-phase system without training data from that system.
references.data: 171 curated reversed-phase RepoRT datasets with condition-disjoint 5-fold CV; human fecal LC-MS/MS case study with 19 NAPS standards as anchors.
references.method: Siamese D-MPNN predicts a retention-order index from structure plus column (HSM/Tanaka) and mobile-phase/pH descriptors. A monotone degree-2 polynomial (LAD outlier removal, then OLS) maps the index to RT using anchors.
references.uncertainty_method: No formal UQ. The RT match threshold for 'almost level 1' was set to the anchor cross-validation MAE (0.40 min).
references.transfer_setting: Target system unseen during training; about 15-30 anchors (high-confidence library hits or standards) fix the mapping.
references.main_results: Condition-awareness lowered retention-order error from 5.61% to 4.89%. Under a realistic split, 2-step beat fine-tuned DeepGCN-RT and RT-Transformer on 5 of 6 datasets; 15 anchors sufficed; 9 of 68 unique library hits matched within 0.40 min.
references.code_available: Yes. github.com/boecker-lab/2-step (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.22093097) and a web app.
references.limitations: No calibrated windows or coverage analysis; reversed-phase only; the threshold heuristic is equated to the MAE.
references.relevance_to_study: Pre-empts much of our base score and calibrant mapping (components i and ii). Our distinct contribution is calibrated, difficulty-normalised conformal windows and the coverage and decoy evaluation.

references.authors: Rakhshaninejad, M.; De Waele, G.; Jürgens, M.; Waegeman, W.
references.title: Reliable Molecular Retrieval from Mass Spectra Using Conformal Prediction
references.venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
references.verification: Crossref record and PubMed PMID 42113637 (abstract) retrieved; title matches. Full text not accessed.
references.category: conformal prediction sets for MS/MS candidate retrieval
references.problem: Turn candidate rankings from MS/MS retrieval into spectrum-specific sets that contain the true molecule with a user-specified probability.
references.data: MassSpecGym benchmark under in-distribution, partially shifted and fully out-of-distribution scenarios.
references.method: Marginal and conditional (group-wise) conformal prediction on fingerprint-similarity candidate rankings.
references.uncertainty_method: Split conformal prediction, with conditional variants (e.g. confidence-based grouping) for subgroup reliability.
references.transfer_setting: Explicit evaluation under distribution shift between calibration and test spectra.
references.main_results: Target coverage with small sets when calibration matches test data; sets grow under shift; conditional conformal improves subgroup reliability, best with confidence-based grouping.
references.limitations: MS/MS only (no RT); requires representative calibration spectra; efficiency degrades under shift.
references.relevance_to_study: Shows conformal candidate sets entering small-molecule MS identification and the value of difficulty-conditional calibration under shift. Complementary to, and combinable with, our RT-window layer.

references.authors: Fadil, F.; Schmidt, T.; Amesoeder, C.; Heckscher, S.; Schoen, M.; Gronwald, W.; Oefner, P.J.; Spang, R.; Dettmer, K.
references.title: FastRet: Fast and Simple Retention Time Prediction in Liquid Chromatography
references.venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling
references.verification: Crossref record (with abstract) and PubMed PMID 42670875 retrieved; title matches. PMC13508770 exists but was not read.
references.category: RT prediction tool with few-metabolite model adjustment
references.problem: Fast RT prediction to support candidate prioritisation in untargeted LC-MS metabolomics, including adaptation to changed chromatographic conditions.
references.data: In-house RP (N = 458), RP-anion-exchange mixed-mode (436) and HILIC (388) sets, the Retip HILIC set (970) and 14 external datasets.
references.method: LASSO and boosted regression trees on molecular descriptors, with selective re-measurement and model adjustment from a few re-measured metabolites.
references.uncertainty_method: None reported (point predictions evaluated by R²).
references.transfer_setting: Model adjustment using 25 RP metabolites measured under six modified chromatographic conditions.
references.main_results: Boosted-tree test R² of 0.86, 0.66 and 0.81. Adjusted models reached R² 0.74-0.84 on unseen metabolites (mean gain 0.22 over from-scratch models). Median held-out R² was 0.59 across 14 external sets.
references.code_available: Yes. CRAN package FastRet; web interface fastret.spang-lab.de.
references.limitations: No uncertainty quantification or filtering evaluation; transfer shown only for modified conditions of one lab's systems.
references.relevance_to_study: A 2026 JCIM example showing few-calibrant adaptation is practical without calibrated windows, the gap our conformal layer fills. Note: no 2026 JCIM paper doing RT-based candidate filtering was found.

pre_empting_work.title: Times are changing but order matters: transferable prediction of small-molecule liquid chromatography retention times (Kretschmer et al., Nat Methods 2026)
pre_empting_work.what_it_preempts: Components (i) and (ii). It learns a condition-aware retention-order index by pairwise (Siamese) ranking on 171 RepoRT RP datasets, using column (HSM/Tanaka) and mobile-phase/pH descriptors with condition-disjoint CV. It then maps the index to RT with a monotone low-order polynomial from about 15-30 anchors. It does not provide calibrated or conformal windows (its RT threshold is the anchor-CV MAE), coverage evaluation, difficulty normalisation or isomeric-decoy elimination.

pre_empting_work.title: Candidate Structure Prioritization in Non-Target Screening with Predicted Collision Cross-Sections and Uncertainty Quantification (Ferrando Plo & Kruve, JCIM 2026)
pre_empting_work.what_it_preempts: The conceptual core of (iii): a normalised Mondrian conformal predictive system whose difficulty function is the MCES distance to training compounds. It includes calibration-conditional validity and conformal OOD detection, and guarantees retention of ≥ 1-α true structures during NTS candidate prioritisation. The authors explicitly propose extending it to retention times. Not covered: RT, chromatographic-system shift with 10-50 in-lab calibrants, jackknife+ with a refitted calibrant mapping, difficulty meta-learned across systems.

pre_empting_work.title: Probabilistic metabolite annotation using retention time prediction and meta-learned projections (García et al., J Cheminform 2022)
pre_empting_work.what_it_preempts: Meta-learning on other chromatographic methods (leave-one-method-out) to calibrate a few-calibrant (10-50) RT projection with predictive uncertainty (Bayesian GP). Also uses interval-score evaluation and uncertainty-aware (z-score) candidate ranking. It lacks distribution-free coverage guarantees and molecule-level difficulty normalisation.

pre_empting_work.title: Liquid-chromatography retention order prediction for metabolite identification (Bach et al., Bioinformatics 2018), extended in Bach et al. 2021 and 2022 (LC-MS2Struct)
pre_empting_work.what_it_preempts: Part of (i): RankSVM retention-order models trained on RT data pooled from different LC systems and used to score candidate structures. No absolute-RT windows or coverage.

pre_empting_work.title: Do experimental projection methods outcompete retention time prediction models in non-target screening? (Malm & Kruve, Analyst 2025)
pre_empting_work.what_it_preempts: Part of the evaluation narrative in (iv): a multi-laboratory (37 RP systems) benchmark of calibrant-based GAM projection vs ML prediction. It shows calibrant RMSE underestimates suspect error and recommends ±2 RMSE from independent QC chemicals. No conformal intervals and no candidate-level coverage or decoy evaluation.

pre_empting_work.title: Evaluation of an Artificial Neural Network Retention Index Model for Chemical Structure Identification in Nontargeted Metabolomics (Samaraweera et al., Anal Chem 2018)
pre_empting_work.what_it_preempts: Novelty-adaptive RI windows (±2SE for training-similar vs ±3SE for dissimilar candidates) and reporting of true-structure loss against a nominal 95% target. Heuristic, single system, no guarantee.

pre_empting_work.title: Reliable Molecular Retrieval from Mass Spectra Using Conformal Prediction (Rakhshaninejad et al., JCIM 2026)
pre_empting_work.what_it_preempts: Any claim to the first conformal candidate sets in small-molecule MS identification, and to difficulty-conditional conformal calibration under shift. MS/MS only, no RT.

pre_empting_work.title: The METLIN small molecule dataset for machine learning-based retention time prediction (Domingo-Almenara et al., Nat Commun 2019)
pre_empting_work.what_it_preempts: Quantifying true-positive loss of RT filters after projection with a small known set (50 molecules), and showing threshold instability across calibrant draws. Heuristic ROC thresholds, no intervals.

pre_empting_work.title: FastRet: Fast and Simple Retention Time Prediction in Liquid Chromatography (Fadil et al., JCIM 2026)
pre_empting_work.what_it_preempts: Adapting an RT model to changed chromatographic conditions from a few (25) re-measured metabolites. No uncertainty quantification.

pre_empting_work.title: Development and application of retention time prediction models in the suspect and non-target screening of emerging contaminants (Aalizadeh et al., J Hazard Mater 2019)
pre_empting_work.what_it_preempts: Data-driven (Monte Carlo) 'acceptable error windows' and applicability domains for predicted tR in suspect/NTS. Fixed, not finite-sample valid, not candidate-adaptive.

facts: Windows of ±2 min are common in environmental suspect screening. An ANN predicted tR within 2 min for 85% of training/verification compounds and 95% of 100 random test compounds (Bade et al., Sci Total Environ 2015, doi:10.1016/j.scitotenv.2015.08.078; Crossref and PubMed verified).

Bijlsma et al. applied predicted-value tolerance filters of RT Δ ≤ 2 min and CCS Δ ≤ 6%, which reduced suspect features by up to 66% (Anal Chem 2019, doi:10.1021/acs.analchem.9b01218; Crossref and PubMed verified).
Song et al. used ΔRT < 2 min between predicted and observed RT to upgrade 153 of 234 level-S2 contaminants to high confidence (Environ Pollut 2024, doi:10.1016/j.envpol.2024.123763; PubMed verified).
Celma et al. reported a 95% deviation of ±2.32 min for their MARS RT model (±4.05% for [M+H]+ CCS) as the window for suspect screening (JCIM 2022, doi:10.1021/acs.jcim.2c00847; PubMed verified).

McEachran et al. tested ±2, ±3 and ±5 min windows on a 45-min run. At ±5 min (about 11% of run time) roughly 20% of candidates were removed while 18/19 (ACD/ChromGenius) and 17/19 (OPERA-RT) true chemicals were kept. At ±3 min OPERA-RT removed 60% vs 40% of candidates but kept only 42% vs 83% of true chemicals. Zero-loss windows would have required 5.06 and 6.5 min, and windows of at least ±5 min were recommended (Talanta 2018, doi:10.1016/j.talanta.2018.01.022; PMC6066181 full text).

Windows are also given as fractions of run time. ACD/ChromGenius and OPERA-RT predicted 95% of RTs within ±15% of run time, and an earlier QSRR predicted 95% within a 2-min window of an 18-min run, about ±11% (as summarised by McEachran et al. 2018).

Metz et al. used RT tolerances of ±0.1 and ±0.5 min (with m/z ±0.1-5 ppm and CCS ±0.1-3%) to compute identification probability. RT alone produced no unique matches at either tolerance (Anal Chem 2025, doi:10.1021/acs.analchem.4c04060; PMC11740175).

PredRet projections between chromatographic systems gave median errors of 0.01-0.28 min and median prediction-interval widths of 0.08-1.86 min, depending on the system pair (Stanstrup et al., Anal Chem 2015, doi:10.1021/acs.analchem.5b02287; PubMed verified).

Kretschmer et al. labelled library hits 'almost level 1' when observed and transferably predicted RT agreed within 0.40 min, a threshold set equal to the anchor cross-validation MAE (9 of 68 unique hits). They also state that RT, as orthogonal information, is required to reach a level 1 identification (Nat Methods 2026, doi:10.1038/s41592-026-03243-2; PMC13736644).

Hupatz et al. prioritised candidates with an RTI-model cut-off of ±2 standardized residuals (CCS within 3%). The RT filter kept 255 of 515 candidates but deprioritised the correct structure for 2 of 10 spiked chemicals (Anal Bioanal Chem 2025, doi:10.1007/s00216-024-05471-x; PMC11700063).

Malm & Kruve define uncertainty limits through RMSE, MAD and the 95th percentile of absolute deviations in RTI units. They recommend estimating RMSE on independent QC chemicals not used to fit the GAM and using ±2 RMSE (about 95% of true RTs) as the window. Their reason: calibrant RMSE correlated weakly with suspect RMSE (R² = 0.30), and suspect RMSE was significantly higher in 535 of 1332 system pairs, up to more than 100-fold (Analyst 2025, doi:10.1039/d5an00323g; PMC12268317).

In the NORMAN data, GAM projection gave an RMSE of 78.1 RTI units (7.8% of the RTI range; 95% of absolute deviations < 175.2). ML prediction plus projection gave 149.0 (95% < 289.8). Projection was significantly better in 71.5% of 1332 system pairs and prediction in 2.4%. Projection was unavailable for 9.8% of suspects eluting outside the calibrant range (Malm & Kruve 2025).

The NORMAN interlaboratory RT data (41 calibrants, 45 suspects, 37 RP systems) can be downloaded as ESI of Malm & Kruve 2025. The Europe PMC endpoint https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC12268317/supplementaryFiles returned a 19.9 MB zip in this session. Inside, AN-150-D5AN00323G-s001.zip holds SI/data/NORMAN_interlab_RT_data.csv (2,238 rows; columns compound, sample_type cal/sus, RT, SMILES, CS_code; 41 calibrants, 41 detected suspects, 37 system codes), Mordred descriptors, the Athens training RTs, projection/prediction result CSVs and R Markdown scripts. AN-150-D5AN00323G-s002.xlsx lists each system's LC instrument, column, stationary phase, mobile phases A/B/C, gradient program and RMSE/MAD/Q95/R2. Direct PMC /bin/ links returned an HTML bot-check page instead of the files.

These RTs come from the NORMAN interlaboratory comparison on quantification (Malm et al., Anal Chem 2024, doi:10.1021/acs.analchem.4c02902; 41 NTS methods from 37 laboratories; 45 spiked compounds and 41 calibrants; Crossref and PubMed verified). Malm & Kruve used 38 systems, of which 37 reversed-phase; one combined RP+HILIC system was excluded. They report 12-39 detected calibrants and 17-40 detected suspects per system, all with acidic aqueous phases (acid alone or acid plus ammonium salt).

The NORMAN RTI (two sets of 18 calibrants per ionisation mode; Aalizadeh et al., Anal Chem 2021, doi:10.1021/acs.analchem.1c02348) rescales RT linearly between the first- and last-eluting calibrant, ignoring gradient nonlinearity. Fitting a GAM on all shared calibrants cut inter-system suspect RMSE from 150.4 to 78.1 RTI units (Malm & Kruve 2025).

Across NORMAN systems, retention-order Spearman correlations ranged from 0.59 to 0.999. Ammonium-salt (higher-pH) mobile phases shifted basic analytes (pKa 3.6-8.1) later and acids earlier than formic-acid systems, and column chemistry (biphenyl, C8, Kinetex EVO vs Eclipse/Poroshell) formed further clusters (Malm & Kruve 2025).

Samaraweera et al. used RI windows of ±2SE (52.4 RIU) for training-similar candidates and ±3SE (78.6 RIU) otherwise, aiming at 95% sensitivity. Observed sensitivity was 87%: 12 of 91 true metabolites were eliminated where 4-5 were expected, while 58% of PubChem false candidates were removed. Widening by 0.5 SE gave 90% sensitivity at 53% specificity (Anal Chem 2018, doi:10.1021/acs.analchem.8b03118; PMC8378237).

Domingo-Almenara et al. projected SMRT-model predictions using 50 known molecules and applied ROC-optimised relative RT-error thresholds (27.5%, 12.5%, 10% and 27.5%). These filtered out 31%, 41%, 36% and 21% of correct identities on four PredRet systems. Thresholds varied markedly between random calibrant draws, and the authors call predicted-experimental RT filtering 'not a robust approach' (Nat Commun 2019, doi:10.1038/s41467-019-13680-7; PMC6925099).

MetFrag 2.2 scores RT through a linear logP-RT fit on user standards (at least ten recommended) and a Gaussian density with σ = 1.5 logP units 'chosen arbitrarily'. The paper notes logP-based prediction errors of over 1 log unit, or up to several minutes of RT window (Ruttkies et al., J Cheminform 2016, doi:10.1186/s13321-016-0115-9; PMC4732001).

Ferrando Plo & Kruve describe relative CCS thresholds (e.g. 2%) as heuristic and lacking statistical foundation. Their conformal predictive system removed about 16% of incorrect candidates while retaining 90% of true structures (at most 8% above random), was applicable in-domain to only 49% (EnvCCS) and 31% (AllCCS) of ions, and they propose extending it to retention times (JCIM 2026, doi:10.1021/acs.jcim.6c02492; PMC13663483).

Typical calibrant or anchor counts in practice are 10-50, so the jackknife+ finite-window requirement n ≥ 1/α - 1 (9 calibrants at α = 0.10, 19 at α = 0.05) falls within this range. Reported counts: 'ten to 50 chemicals' for projection GAMs (Malm & Kruve 2025); at least 10 standards for MetFrag's logP-RT model (Ruttkies 2016); 10-50 calibrants for meta-learned GP projection (García et al. 2022, doi:10.1186/s13321-022-00613-8); at least 15, about 30 recommended, anchors for 2-step (Kretschmer 2026); 35 calibrants for post-projection calibration with median error < 3.2% of elution time (Zhang et al., Commun Chem 2024, doi:10.1038/s42004-024-01135-0).

García et al. showed that a Bayesian GP projection meta-learned on other chromatographic methods works with as few as 10 calibrants. Ranking by z = |y - μ|/σ put the correct molecule in the top three for 68% of mass queries (J Cheminform 2022; PMC9172150).

Ngan et al. used the discrepancy between structure-predicted and spectrum (CNL)-predicted RTI as a classifier feature, with no measured RT. The structure-to-RTI MAE rose from 89.5 to 111.2 RTI units (MRE 27.5%) on 1237 untrained calibrants, and P(TP) ≥ 0.5 gave a 98.8% TP rate at a 23.4% FP rate (Anal Chem 2025, doi:10.1021/acs.analchem.5c01873; PMC12392258).

Osipenko et al. projected METLIN-trained RT predictions to nano-HPLC using a few compounds (median absolute error < 155 s, 10.8%). ROC-derived filter thresholds eliminated on average 25-42% of false positives (Anal Bioanal Chem 2020, doi:10.1007/s00216-020-02905-0; PubMed verified).

Creek et al. showed that a six-descriptor HILIC QSRR built on 120 standards removed 40% of the false identifications made by accurate mass alone (Anal Chem 2011, doi:10.1021/ac2021823; PubMed verified).

Condition-aware retention-order indices lowered pairwise order error from 5.61% to 4.89% across 171 RepoRT RP datasets. 2-step outperformed fine-tuned DeepGCN-RT and RT-Transformer on 5 of 6 targets under a realistic split, with 15 anchors sufficient for the RT mapping (Kretschmer et al., Nat Methods 2026).

LC-MS2Struct improved state-of-the-art MS2 scorers by up to 106% on 4,327 MassBank molecules from 18 LC conditions by exploiting observed retention orders (Bach et al., Nat Mach Intell 2022, doi:10.1038/s42256-022-00577-2).

No 2026 JCIM paper on RT-based candidate filtering was found. The closest 2026 JCIM papers are Ferrando Plo & Kruve (conformal CCS prioritisation that explicitly proposes an RT extension), Fadil et al. (FastRet RT prediction for candidate prioritisation) and Rakhshaninejad et al. (conformal MS/MS retrieval). A 2026 news interview claim that RT filtering removes more than 40% of incorrect candidates could not be traced to a paper and was not used.
